title: GRAVITY and FEROS/ESPRESSO data from 2015-2025 resolve the HD 93683 third star: a Be star on a 2.44-yr orbit that drives the eclipse loss only if it has at least 17 percent of the mass
abstract: HD 93683 is an eclipsing O9V+B0V pair (P = 17.8 d) whose eclipses faded from 1990 to 2026 through an inclination drift of -0.33 deg/yr. Prior campaign studies gave conditional bounds that require a third body on an orbit of a few years and asked for velocities or astrometry. We analysed public ESO archive data: VLTI/GRAVITY interferometry at 9 epochs (2022-2024) and 23 FEROS and ESPRESSO spectra (2015-2025). GRAVITY closure phases resolve the eclipsing pair at 0.5-1.6 mas from the brightest K-band source and also show a faint companion at 108 mas. At every epoch the Br-gamma photocentre shift points away from the pair, so the brightest source is the Be star. The Be-star Fe II emission velocities and the relative astrometry independently select the same orbit: P = 890.5 +- 0.7 d, e = 0.344 +- 0.008, i = 77.4 +- 0.6 deg, a = 2.74 +- 0.08 mas, K = 58.1 +- 0.7 km/s. The orbit predicted the position at a held-out epoch (2023-01-20, two files) to 0.07 and 0.27 mas. The mass function is 15.0 +- 0.6 solar masses. With B the mass fraction of the pair, m(pair) = 16.1/B^2 solar masses and the distance is 1.67/B kpc; the Gaia DR3 parallax (0.886 mas, RUWE 3.1) is excluded. N-body integrations of the measured orbit reach the observed drift only for B <= 0.83, so m(Be) >= 4.9 and m(pair) >= 23.5 solar masses, and the distance is >= 2.0 kpc. At the Carina distance (an assumption) B = 0.71, m(pair) = 32 and m(Be) = 13 solar masses. Main limitation: the reflex motion against the wide companion gives B = 0.905 +- 0.033, in conflict with the drift limit and the light ratio; we cannot find the cause. He II systemic velocities of the pair are dominated by systematics. The next eclipse season is not fixed (2065-2380). We give testable positions and velocities for 2027-2029.
